e.t: This word means “to do wrong” or “to harm.” It describes an action that injures, mistreats, or acts unjustly toward another person. As a verb, it focuses on what someone does rather than merely on the condition or result of wrongdoing. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 28 times, showing repeated use for harmful or unjust actions in both personal disputes and broader moral warnings.

This word describes something disgraceful or shameful—conduct, speech, or a condition that brings dishonor. It points to what is improper and exposed as morally embarrassing rather than worthy of respect. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times, appearing in passages that use this language to identify behavior or matters that should not be treated as honorable. Its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central sense remains clear: something shameful, dishonoring, or disgraceful.

This word means “proportion”: a measured share or fitting relationship between things. In the Greek New Testament, it appears once, in Romans 12:6. It is best understood as language describing how something corresponds appropriately to something else. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the central idea is a fitting measure, relationship, or share rather than something unrelated or excessive.

e.t: This word describes actively struggling against someone or something. It conveys resistance and determined effort in opposition, rather than merely facing difficulty or experiencing a passive conflict. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, so its normal meaning is established by this focused use: to struggle or to struggle against. The exact force in Hebrews 12:4 depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but the word itself points to strenuous opposition and perseverance in the face of resistance.

e.t: This word means “to register” or “to take a census.” It describes recording people in an official enrollment or count. In the Greek New Testament, it appears four times, chiefly in Luke’s account of people being registered, and once in Hebrews. Its central idea is organized registration: people are entered into an official record rather than merely counted informally. The precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but the word consistently points to formal enrollment or census-taking.

e.t: This word means “to restore” or “to restore” something—to bring it back to its proper condition, place, or function. It is a verb describing an act of making something whole or right again. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs eight times, including passages where restoration is spoken of as something that happens to a person or condition. Its basic sense remains focused on returning something to what it should be.

This word describes someone or something that is disappearing—becoming unseen or no longer visible. It expresses the removal of visible presence rather than simply being absent. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Luke 24:31, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its central idea remains clear: something visible is no longer seen, as it vanishes from sight.

e.t: This word means “to sound” or “to take a sounding”—to measure the depth of water, usually by lowering a line or sounding device. It describes a practical action used to determine how deep the sea is, rather than a general noise or musical sound. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both within one verse in Acts, where its normal sense concerns checking water depth. The exact force in that verse is clarified by the surrounding passage, but the word itself points to measuring depth in the water.

This word means “knowledge”—what is known or understood. In the Greek New Testament, it refers to knowledge as something people may possess, receive, increase, or lack. It can concern God’s ways, spiritual instruction, or truths that shape how believers live. The word occurs 29 times in 28 New Testament verses, including passages in Luke, Romans, and the Corinthian letters. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding context.

e.t: This word means “be away” or “to be away.” It describes being absent from a place rather than physically present there. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, all in 2 Corinthians 5:6, 5:8, and 5:9. Its basic sense is straightforward: a person is away or absent, while the surrounding sentence determines what place or presence is being contrasted. The word itself expresses location or absence, not a separate quality or action.

This word means “free,” describing someone who is not under another person’s ownership, control, or obligation as a slave. It can identify a person’s social status, as when someone is contrasted with a slave, and it can describe release from a former condition. The word occurs 23 times in the Greek New Testament, including passages concerning family status, slavery, and freedom. Its central idea is liberty or the condition of being free, while the surrounding sentence determines whether it refers to social standing or release from a particular obligation.

e.t: This word means “to dress” or “to put on,” describing the act of clothing someone or putting clothing on oneself. It is an action word focused on wearing garments rather than on the garments themselves. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, in Mark 15:17 and Luke 16:19. The surrounding verse supplies the details of who is dressed and what is worn, but the word itself expresses the act of clothing. Its basic sense is straightforward: to put clothing on or be dressed.

This word means “clothing,” referring to garments worn on the body. It is an ordinary word for what a person wears, whether considered as a needed provision, an outward appearance, or an item of dress. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs eight times in eight verses—seven in Matthew and once in Luke. Its basic meaning remains straightforward: clothing or garments; the precise point being made depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

e.t: This word means “to spring up” or “to sprout up.” It describes something rising and beginning to grow, especially like a plant emerging from the ground. As a verb, it expresses the action of coming up rather than simply naming a plant or growth. It occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, once in Matthew and once in Mark, showing the same basic action in both passages.

This word means a worker: a person who labors or carries out assigned work. It can describe workers generally, including people laboring in a field or other setting. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 16 times across 15 verses, from Matthew through James. Its basic meaning remains focused on the person doing the work, while the surrounding passage determines what kind of work or responsibility is in view.

e.t: This word means “to dress”—to put clothing on or get oneself clothed. It describes the ordinary action of dressing rather than naming a particular garment. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times in two verses. The surrounding passage determines who is dressing and what circumstances are involved, but the word itself points to the act of putting on clothes. It does not, by itself, identify a specific garment or add a wider meaning beyond dressing.

Joel is a personal name, identifying someone named Joel rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek New Testament, this name appears once, in Acts 2:16. The available wording preserves the name as “Joel,” so its ordinary function is simply to identify a person by name. The name’s significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself is a proper name rather than a general vocabulary term.

This word describes one who knows the heart— the inner person, including what is held within. It is a title or description for a heart-knower rather than a general term for outward observation. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both in Acts, where it identifies the one able to know the human heart. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage context.

This word refers to a place where guests stay, such as a guest room or an inn. It can describe lodging within a household or a place intended for travelers, with the surrounding passage determining the precise setting. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times: once in Mark and twice in Luke. Its basic idea is a room or lodging space made available to guests, rather than a person who is visiting.

This word means “seed,” referring to a small grain that can be planted and grow into a plant. It names the seed itself rather than the completed plant or harvest. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs seven times across seven verses, appearing in Matthew, Mark, Luke, John, and 1 Corinthians. Its ordinary sense provides the basis for scriptural comparisons involving small beginnings, planting, growth, and eventual results.

This word means “crystal,” referring to a clear, glasslike mineral or crystal substance. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Revelation. It describes something associated with striking clarity and brightness, but its exact significance in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and vision. The word itself identifies the material or appearance, rather than expressing an action, emotion, or moral quality.

This Greek New Testament word refers chiefly to a lamp, while it can also mean a window. It names a physical object associated with light or visibility. It occurs nine times in the Greek New Testament, including several occurrences in Matthew 25 concerning lamps and one in John 18. Its exact sense is determined by the surrounding sentence, but the central idea is an object that gives or admits light.

Luke is a personal name, referring to an individual identified by that name in the Greek New Testament. It is not a description of an action, quality, or object, but a proper name used to identify a person. The name appears three times in the Greek New Testament: in Colossians, 2 Timothy, and Philemon. Its precise role in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This word refers to a meat market—the place where meat was sold. It is a noun naming a public marketplace rather than describing an action, person, or spiritual quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Corinthians 10:25. Its basic meaning is straightforward, while the surrounding passage determines how that marketplace fits into Paul’s instruction. The word itself identifies the setting where meat could be purchased; it does not, by itself, state anything about the buyer, the seller, or the meat’s religious significance.

e.t: This word means “to blame” or “to criticize,” describing the act of finding fault with someone. It expresses a negative judgment directed toward a person or their conduct, rather than simply noticing a weakness. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times in 2 Corinthians. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains assigning fault or exposing grounds for criticism.

Nicopolis is a proper place-name, rendered as “Nicopolis.” It identifies a location rather than describing an action, quality, or person. In the Greek New Testament, this word occurs once, in Titus 3:12. Because no verse text or surrounding passage is included here, its specific importance in that passage must be understood from the context of Titus. The word itself simply names Nicopolis. “Nicopolis” is the consistent English rendering provided for this name.

This word refers to a mountain or hill, an elevated area of land. It can describe one such place or several, with the Greek New Testament rendering it as “mountain,” “mountains,” or “hill.” Its meaning remains a straightforward geographic term, while the surrounding verse determines how that place functions in a particular passage. The word occurs 63 times in the Greek New Testament, from Matthew through Revelation, showing regular use for mountainous or elevated terrain rather than a rare or specialized expression.

This Greek New Testament word means “no” or “not.” It is a negative word used to deny, reject, or mark something as untrue within a sentence or question. Its basic function remains consistent wherever it appears: it reverses or excludes the statement it accompanies. This word occurs 70 times in the Greek New Testament, showing that it is a regularly used expression of negation rather than a word limited to one setting.

e.t: This word means “to observe” or “to watch closely,” describing deliberate attention to someone or something. It points to careful monitoring rather than a passing glance. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs six times. It expresses attentive action, not merely awareness, and the surrounding passage determines the precise object and purpose of that observation. Its central idea remains sustained, close watching wherever it appears.

e.t: This word means “to encircle” or “to surround,” describing something being enclosed on every side. It presents surrounding as an action that closes in around a person, place, or thing. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Luke 19:43. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense is clear: to form a boundary around something so that it is enclosed or hemmed in.

This word means “what?” and is used to ask for the identity, nature, or choice of something. It functions as a question word, directing attention to the thing being discussed rather than stating the answer itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 33 times in 32 verses, appearing in questions across Matthew, Mark, Luke, John, Acts, and Revelation. Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding question and subject.

e.t: This word means “predicted,” “to foretell,” or “to predict”—to announce something beforehand. It describes speaking about an event or outcome before it happens, so its central idea is a prior announcement rather than a present observation. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs nine times across nine verses, including passages in the Gospels, Paul’s letters, Hebrews, Peter, and Jude. Its exact force in a verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word refers to a “place of honor”—a position given special recognition. It names a location associated with distinction rather than an ordinary place, especially when people are arranged or invited according to status. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs five times in five verses. Its central idea is the honored place someone seeks, is offered, or occupies. The surrounding passage determines whether the word emphasizes the physical place or the honor represented by it.

Sharon is a place name, referring to a location named Sharon. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 9:35. Because the word itself is a proper name rather than a description or action, its basic meaning is the identification of that place. The surrounding verse and passage provide the details about what happened there, while the name itself simply identifies Sharon.

e.t: This word means “to have compassion on” or “to pity.” It describes an inward response of mercy toward someone who is suffering, needy, helpless, or facing trouble. In the New Testament, it is used of compassionate action or merciful response rather than mere awareness of another person’s pain. The word occurs 12 times in the Greek New Testament, especially in Matthew, Mark, and Luke. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains a moved heart that responds with pity and compassion.

This word means “chest,” referring to the front or upper part of the body. It is a concrete noun used for a person’s physical chest, including the area where someone may lean, rest, or be struck. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs five times, in Luke, John, and Revelation. Its references include descriptions of people placing themselves against another’s chest and of figures clothed in garments reaching to the chest. The exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word describes someone who is a co-member of a body, belonging to the same body as others. It expresses shared membership and unity rather than separate or independent belonging. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Ephesians 3:6, and its basic sense is “co-member of a body” or “of the same body.” The surrounding passage determines how this shared membership is applied in that verse.

Tyre is the name of a city mentioned in the Greek New Testament. The word functions as a place name rather than describing an action, quality, or spiritual condition. It appears eleven times in eleven New Testament verses, including passages that mention Tyre alongside other places or refer to people from that region. Its ordinary meaning is therefore the geographical name Tyre; the particular significance of its mention depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This Greek New Testament word means “a son” or “son.” It identifies a male child and can be used for one son or for sons. The word is widely used across the New Testament, occurring 377 times in 344 verses, from Matthew through Revelation. Its ordinary meaning is straightforward, while the surrounding words determine whose son is being named or described in a particular passage. Scripture renders it chiefly as “Son” or “sons.”

Hypocrisy means presenting a false appearance of goodness or sincerity while the heart or conduct does not match that appearance. It describes a divided life in which outward words, religious behavior, or public actions conceal a contrary inner reality. In the Greek New Testament, the word is used six times and is consistently rendered “hypocrisy.” It identifies a serious mismatch between what a person appears to be and what that person truly is, rather than merely describing weakness or an occasional mistake.

e.t: This word means to fear—to experience dread, apprehension, or alarm, and it can describe someone who fears or is afraid. In the New Testament, it is used for the inward response of fearing as well as the expressed action of being afraid. It appears 95 times in the Greek New Testament, showing a broad use across its writings. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding context and what or whom the person fears.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to lead by the hand.” It describes guiding a person by taking or holding the hand, so the word functions as an action of physically directing someone. It occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, both times in Acts: 9:8 and 22:11. The basic sense is concrete and straightforward: one person is led or guided by another through the hand.

This word means “dust,” referring to the fine particles or loose earth found on the ground. It is a noun naming a physical substance. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice: once in Mark and once in Revelation, with both occurrences rendered “dust.” The word can therefore describe something ordinary and earthly, whether associated with the ground or with material scattered from it. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This word means “gold,” the valuable metal used to describe material wealth, treasured objects, or something made from gold. It is a straightforward noun naming the substance itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 10 times in 9 verses, including passages in Matthew, Acts, 1 Corinthians, James, and Revelation. Its normal meaning remains consistent wherever it appears; the surrounding verse determines whether the focus is the metal, an object made from it, or its value.

This word means “little faith” or “littleness of faith.” It describes faith as limited or insufficient in measure, drawing attention to how small a person’s trust is rather than denying that faith exists at all. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Matthew 17:20. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself focuses on the smallness or inadequacy of faith.

e.t: This word means “exceedingly” or “greatly,” intensifying the action or description it accompanies. It points to something occurring to an unusually high degree, rather than merely marking ordinary strength or extent. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times in 2 Corinthians. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic function is to emphasize an exceptional degree or magnitude.
